books.section: The Jackson Presidency and Jacksonian Democracy

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 13, and Princeton Review, Chapter 8: In earlier elections, congressional caucuses chose the parties' nominees, and electors were often chosen by state legislatures. In 1800, only five states let voters choose presidential electors directly; by 1824, 18 of 24 states did so. When the Democratic-Republican caucus chose William H. Crawford in 1824, Adams, Clay, and Jackson all challenged the nomination, and attacks on the caucus as undemocratic brought the caucus system down. Jackson believed his supporters should take over federal offices held by Adams's partisans, holding that any reasonably capable citizen could do a government job. Trading jobs for political favors came to be known as the spoils system.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 13 (“The Election of 1824”; “President Jackson”) and Princeton Review, Chapter 8 (“The Jackson Presidency and Jacksonian Democracy”). Paraphrased, not quoted.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Jackson's defense of the spoils system rested on which belief?

options.text: Only trained experts should hold government jobs
options.misconception: Jackson held the opposite: any reasonably capable citizen could do the job.

options.text: Government offices should pass from father to son
options.misconception: Jackson wanted rotation in office, not inheritance.

options.text: Ordinary citizens could do government jobs without special expertise
Offices should go to the wealthiest citizens
options.misconception: Jackson presented himself as the champion of the common man, not of the wealthy.

rationales.A: Jackson said the opposite: ordinary citizens could do the work.
rationales.B: Jackson favored rotation in office, not inheritance.
rationales.C: Jackson held that any reasonably capable and well-informed citizen could perform the duties of a government job.
rationales.D: Jackson claimed to speak for the common man, not the wealthy.
rationales.general:
1. Find his reason. Jackson said any reasonably capable citizen could do a government job.
2. Follow it. If no special expertise is needed, then giving jobs to supporters is fair, not corrupt.
3. See the other side. Critics called it cronyism and named it the spoils system.
Background: Jackson replaced many of Adams's officeholders with his own supporters when he took office in 1829.
Remember: a practice looks fair or foul depending on what you think the job needs.
